new_statements.quote: [p. 497] Les données sont regroupées sous les rubriques suivantes : 1. opposition de longueur réalisée 2. opposition de longueur sous-jacente 3. système tonal ou accentuel 4. nombre de schèmes prosodiques des thèmes nominaux dissyllabiques 5. liste des schèmes 6. présence ou absence de la règle de Meeussen [...] 10. statut de la syllabe pénultième. [p. 513] Gweno : 1. : non 2. : non ? 3. : langue tonale 4. : 4 5. : -cvcv, -cv́cv, -cvcv́, -cv́cv́ 6. : absente ? (7) 8. : condition générala [sic] 9. : post-lexical : HBB > HHB 10. : accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)
new_statements.translation: [p. 497] The data are grouped under the following headings: 1. surface length contrast 2. underlying length contrast 3. tonal or accentual system 4. number of prosodic patterns of disyllabic noun stems 5. list of the patterns 6. presence or absence of Meeussen's rule [...] 10. status of the penultimate syllable. [p. 513] Gweno: 1: no; 2: no?; 3: tone language; 4: 4; 5: -cvcv, -cv́cv, -cvcv́, -cv́cv́; 6: absent?; (7); 8: general condition; 9: post-lexical: HLL > HHL; 10: demarcative accent (culmination of length) [i.e. on the penultimate syllable].
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de doctorat d'État, Université Paris V. Annexe: Résumé des systèmes prosodiques, key p. 497, Groupe XXI 'Gweno' entry p. 513.

new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked:, Philippson 1991 'Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale', DDL Lyon open fulltext (the PDF's metadata gives the author 'Gerard Philippson', 2003 distill of the thesis). (1) Locator check: PDF p. 497 (the text layer) carries the annex heading 'ANNEXE : RESUME DES SYSTEMES PROSODIQUES' and the ten-rubric key exactly as quoted (rubrics 7-9, elided by the reader with [..], are '7. modalites d'application de la regle 8. RIAT 9. principales regles prosodiques ulterieures'); PDF p. 513 (extracted text, the text layer) carries the Gweno entry character-for-character: '1. : non / 2. : non ? / 3. : langue tonale / 4. : 4 / 5. : -cvcv, -c&vcv, -cvc&v, -c&vc&v / 6. : ab…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gweno is a High/Low tone language (four lexical tone patterns on disyllabic noun stems, no vowel-length contrast, tone doubling as the main tone rule); independently of tone, the penultimate syllable carries a non-distinctive demarcative accent realised as lengthening (culmination of length). No lexical/contrastive stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for the penultimate accent; the entry hedges only on underlying length ('non ?') and Meeussen's rule ('absente ?'). Philippson & Nurse 2000 sec. 2.2-2.3 (the fuller Gweno sketch) describe all vowels as short and treat only tone, without repeating the penult-lengthening remark.
new_statements.domain_note: Philippson's 'accent démarcatif' is a boundary-marking (demarcative) prominence; his general discussion (p. 486) describes the penultimate lengthening in these Eastern Bantu languages as marking the end of the word/prosodic group before pause, 'plus ou moins nette selon les langues'. The Gweno annex entry does not specify word vs phrase; data are Philippson's own field recordings (1970s UDSM consultant, 1988, 1991 Ugweno Division).
new_statements.identity_note: Both Philippson sources describe Gweno proper (E65, own name kiɣonu, Ugweno Division, North Pare Mountains) = Glottolog gwen1239; Philippson & Nurse note minor internal dialect divisions (Ngofi at the northern tip) but base the description on several Ugweno villages. Not to be confused with Asu/Chasu (Pare, G22, asup1239), in which Gweno speakers are bilingual and whose tone system Gweno's resembles.

new_statements.quote: Where the accent is not marked, it generally falls on the penultimate.
new_statements.citation: Johnston, Harry Hamilton (1885). The Kilima-Njaro expedition: a record of scientific exploration in eastern equatorial Africa, and a general description of the natural history, languages, and commerce of the Kilima-Njaro District. Proceedings of the Royal Geographical Society and monthly record of geography 7. Kegan Paul & Trench. xv, 572 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 477 (last sentence of the orthography note, 'Languages of the Kilima-njaro District', Chapter XX); referred to from Appendix II p. 521 'Vocabularies of Ki-caga, Ki-gweno, and Ki-taveita: For explanation of Orthography, see the preceding remarks on pp. 476, 477' and from p. 495 ('For the system of orthography used in spelling these languages, I would refer the reader to the explanation given on page 476'). line 24203; verified on the page image.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: ' and the page image shows it as the last sentence of p. 477 ('LANGUAGES OF THE KILIMA-NJARO DISTRICT. 477'), closing the Lepsius-alphabet orthography note. Scope confirmed from p. 476 (line 24048-24052): 'The mode of spelling adopted in these and other vocabularies which follow, and throughout the volume where African names are introduced.. is practically the same as that proposed in Lepsius' Standard Alphabet' - a blanket convention introduced for the Masai vocabulary; p. 495 (line 24989-24991) refers the Bantu vocabularies (Ki-caga, Ki-gweno, Ki-taveita) to 'the explanation given on page 476 in connection with the Masai vocabulary'; Appendix II p. 521 (line 29955-29956, page image) 'For…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penultimate) but weak evidence: an 1885 explorer's blanket orthographic remark covering every vocabulary in the volume, not a description of Gweno prosody; Johnston says nothing about tone, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Philippson 1991's 'langue tonale + accent demarcatif (culmination de longueur)' profile, which already implies penultimate prominence via length. Note the listed HathiTrust copy (mdp.39015011941567, rights pd/Full view per the catalog API) could not be reached by automated download 'Blocked from HathiTrust' on both attempts; the same edition was read from archive.org (kilimanjaroexpe00john, Smithsonian Libraries scan, + page image…
new_statements.rule_in_words: An orthographic convention for all the vocabularies in the book (Masai and the Bantu languages of Kilima-njaro, the Ki-gweno wordlist included by explicit cross-reference): unless an accent is written on the word, the stress is on the penultimate syllable. It is not a Gweno-specific phonological statement; the Gweno column of Appendix II is a thin wordlist with occasional marked accents (e.g. 'Niru'u, 5' banana, p. 521).
new_statements.exceptions: 'generally' - words with a written accent mark are stressed where marked; no Gweno examples discussed. The separate Masai statement (p. 454: 'The accent in Masai falls occasionally (especially in derivatives) on the first syllable of the word (generally the root), most frequently on the penultimate, and rarely on the last') concerns Masai, not Gweno. Nothing on tone for any language.
new_statements.identity_note: Johnston's 'Ki-gweno' is the language of the Ugweno mountains south of Lake Jipe (p. 494: 'Ki-gweno closely resembles Ki-caga. It is the dialect of the Ugweno mountains to the south of Lake Jipe'), i.e. the Gweno of gwen1239; his Ki-gweno column ('Ki-gweno, &c.') also carries Ki-kamba, Masai, Ki-taita, Zulu and Lu-ganda comparanda, so individual entries must be checked for the language label.

sources.note: Annexe 'Résumé des systèmes prosodiques' (key p. 497; Gweno entry p. 513): Gweno = 'langue tonale', no length contrast, 4 tonal schemes on disyllabic noun stems, and under rubric 10 'statut de la syllabe pénultième': 'accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)'. Tableau II p. 78 classes Gweno '(a):4, (b):2' (tonal, not accentual); ch. 4 sec. 2.2 pp. 87-90 gives Gweno tone association / tone-doubling rules from Philippson's own field data; p. 487 puts Gweno at 'stade I' (tonal assimilation without neutralisation), unlike Kilimanjaro Chaga which superimposed a Kamba-like accentual system.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2 Vowels: five vowels 'all short'; sec. 2.3 Suprasegmentals treats tone only: 'Basically, Gweno distinguishes High.. and Low tones', tones stay on their vowel (no tone shift, unlike other Chaga), the practically only tone process is Tone Doubling (H spreads one syllable right unless before H or pause), with downstep in faster speech. No statement about stress, accent or penultimate lengthening anywhere in the sketch (a full-text search for stress/accent/penult: only tone-diacritic and 'it must be stressed that' hits).
